content: 1. All vaccines must be administered strictly according to the specifications provided in the product label or package insert. 2. The list of vaccines in Part III includes all vaccines licensed by the USDA and marketed in the United States at the time of publication. Any new vaccine approvals or changes to label specifications made after publication should also be considered part of this list. 3. Any vaccine listed can be used for revaccination, even if it is not the same brand as the previously administered vaccine. 4. Vaccines used in state and local rabies control programs should provide immunity for a duration of three years. This approach is the most effective method to increase the proportion of immunized dogs and cats in a population. 5. There is no laboratory or epidemiologic evidence to support the annual or biennial administration of three-year vaccines following the initial series. 6. Currently, there is no epidemiologic association between any specific licensed vaccine product and adverse events, including vaccine failure. 7. The efficacy of parenteral rabies vaccination in wildlife and hybrid animals (offspring of wild animals crossbred with domestic animals) has not been established, and no vaccine is licensed for these animals. 8. Zoos or research institutions may establish vaccination programs to protect valuable animals, but these programs should not replace public health measures designed to protect humans, such as wound treatment and the administration of human rabies immune globulin and vaccine. 9. Recommendations for pre-exposure and post-exposure rabies prophylaxis, including details of their administration, are available in the current guidelines of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). These guidelines also provide information on the local and regional status of animal rabies and the availability of human rabies biologics. 10. Rabies vaccinations may be administered under the supervision of a veterinarian to animals held in animal control shelters before their release. Veterinarians signing a rabies certificate must ensure that the person administering the vaccine is identified on the certificate and is appropriately trained in vaccine storage, handling, administration, and management of adverse events. 11. Within 28 days after primary vaccination, an animal reaches a peak rabies antibody titer and can be considered immunized. An animal is considered currently vaccinated if the primary vaccination was administered at least 28 days prior and subsequent vaccinations have been given according to the guidelines. 12. Regardless of the age of the animal at initial vaccination, a booster vaccination should be administered one year later. Following a booster vaccination, an animal is considered currently vaccinated immediately due to the expected rapid anamnestic response. 13. Protocols for post-exposure vaccination of previously unvaccinated domestic animals have not been validated, and evidence suggests that vaccine use alone will not prevent the disease. 14. Dogs, cats, and ferrets that are currently vaccinated should be revaccinated immediately, kept under the owner’s control, and observed for 45 days. 15. All species of livestock are susceptible to rabies, with cattle and horses being the most frequently infected. Livestock exposed to a rabid animal and currently vaccinated with a USDA-approved vaccine for that species should be revaccinated immediately and observed for 45 days. 16. Unvaccinated livestock exposed to rabies should be slaughtered immediately. If the owner is unwilling to do so, the animal should be kept under close observation for six months. 17. If unvaccinated livestock is slaughtered within seven days of being bitten, its tissues may be consumed without risk of infection, provided that liberal portions of the exposed area are discarded. Federal guidelines require that any animal known to have been exposed to rabies within eight months be rejected for slaughter. 18. Neither tissues nor milk from a rabid animal should be used for human or animal consumption. Pasteurization temperatures inactivate the rabies virus, so drinking pasteurized milk or eating cooked meat does not constitute rabies exposure. 19. Having more than one rabid animal in a herd or herbivore-to-herbivore transmission is uncommon, so restricting the rest of the herd if a single animal has been exposed to or infected by rabies may not be necessary. 20. The use of licensed oral vaccines for mass vaccination of free-ranging wildlife should be considered in specific situations with the approval of the state agency responsible for animal rabies control. Distribution of oral rabies vaccines should be based on scientific assessments of the target species and followed by timely analysis of surveillance data, with results shared with stakeholders. 21. Continuous programs for trapping or poisoning wildlife are not effective in reducing wildlife rabies reservoirs on a statewide basis. However, selective removal of high-risk wildlife species may be indicated in certain areas, such as picnic grounds, camps, or suburban regions. 22. State agriculture, public health, and wildlife agencies should be consulted for planning, coordination, and evaluation of vaccination or population reduction programs. 23. Indigenous rabid bats have been reported in every state except Hawaii and have caused rabies in at least 40 humans in the United States. Bats should be excluded from houses, public buildings, and adjacent structures to prevent direct association with humans. 24. Structures should be made bat-proof by sealing entrances used by bats. Controlling rabies in bats through programs designed to reduce bat populations is neither feasible nor desirable.
